title: Scaffold and mobile tower checks before use
audience: Workers and supervisors who use, move or check scaffolds and mobile towers on trade and exterior jobs.
learningOutcomes: Identify who may erect, alter and dismantle a scaffold or a mobile tower, and when specialist authority is needed.
Check a mobile tower before climbing: ground, verticality, outriggers, castors, brakes, platform boarding and tag.
Identify scaffold defects that stop use, including gaps, missing guardrails and the toe boards, an unstable base and unsafe access.
Explain why tagging, handover certificates and inspection records are part of the safety control.

instruction.heading: What a scaffold is for
instruction.body: A scaffold is a temporary framework that people stand on or work from, or that gives access to a work position. The sources in this pack describe several types, including independent tied, mobile, free-standing, system and tube-and-fitting scaffolds. The common hazards are collapse, gaps in the platform, contact with overhead electrical lines, unauthorised access, untrained erection, falling objects and an incomplete structure. A mobile tower is a single unit on castors. It is quick to set up, but it can tip if its base, load or height is wrong.

instruction.heading: Who builds and changes a scaffold
instruction.body: Erecting, altering and dismantling a scaffold are specialist tasks. One source says these should be done only by a qualified scaffold erector. In New South Wales, only licensed scaffolders may erect, alter or dismantle a scaffold where the fall risk exceeds four metres; that rule is confirmed in the project licence matrix. Do not remove ties, braces, guardrails or boards to make a task easier. One source warns that tampering with scaffold components can lead to prosecution and fines, and the same principle applies in any state.

instruction.heading: Tags and handover
instruction.body: A scaffold should carry a tag showing whether it can be used safely, who checked it and when. A competent individual should check a new or changed scaffold before it is used, and the handover should come with a completion certificate. A tag that is out of date, missing or red means the scaffold is not used until a competent individual has checked it again.

instruction.heading: Walk the scaffold before use
instruction.body: Walk the whole structure before the first use each day, and again after any change, impact or storm. Check the base is level and stable and that the uprights are vertical. Check that every horizontal member is rigid at each joint, and that diagonal bracing is in place. The platform must be fully boarded, the boards secured, and there must be no gap through which a person or tool could fall. Check the handrails, the mid-rails and the toe boards at every open edge, and check that access is by a suitable ladder that extends above the landing, not by climbing the frame. Look for overhead lines, unsafe fixings and anything hanging from the structure.

instruction.heading: Mobile towers
instruction.body: A mobile tower is often safer than a ladder, and the sources recommend one where safer access is not available. Before erection, check that the castors roll freely, that the components are sound, and that the brakes and locks work. On a suspended floor, check that the floor can carry the load. Before use, the tower must be vertical and square, the platform must be fully boarded, the outriggers placed properly and locked in position, the wheels locked, and the tower tagged. The sources give a height above which stabilisers are required and another above which the tower is tied off, and they require the aluminium quantity schedule from the maker to be followed. The control is what matters: stabilise and tie the tower where the maker and the risk assessment require it.

instruction.heading: Moving a tower
instruction.body: Do not move a tower with anyone on it unless the maker allows it and the surface is clear. Lock the wheels before anyone climbs. Keep the surface flat and finished, because a rough or sloped surface changes the risk of tipping. Come down before any movement, and check the tower again when it is set back up.

instruction.heading: Records
instruction.body: Keep the erection certificate, the tags, the inspection records and the component list for each scaffold or tower. One source expects an inspection at regular intervals, recorded on a form.

procedure: Confirm the scaffold or tower was erected by a person with the right authority, and that the tag and certificate are present.
Walk the structure: base, verticality, bracing and joints.
Check the platform: boards, fixings, gaps and damaged boards.
Check the guardrails, the mid-rails and the toe boards along every open edge.
Check the access route and the overhead services.
For a mobile tower, check the castors, brakes, outriggers, stabilisers and surface before anyone climbs.
Tag the structure as safe to use, or stop and report it.
Repeat the check after weather, impact or any change.

workedExamples.situation: A painter finds a mobile tower with one castor not locked, standing on a slight slope, with platform boards laid unevenly.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the tower be used as it is?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The slope and the unlocked castor mean the tower may move and tip. The surface is corrected or the tower is moved to a level area, the castors are locked, the platform is re-boarded, and the tag is checked before anyone climbs.

workedExamples.situation: A scaffold tag is green but dated before the last check, and a guardrail is missing on one side.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop use. The tag date is outside the check interval the business uses, and the missing rail means the scaffold cannot be treated as safe. The supervisor is told, and a competent individual re-checks the scaffold before anyone uses it.

equipmentAndPpe: Spirit level or plumb check tool
Stabilisers and outriggers as the maker specifies
Hard hat with chin strap where objects can fall

commonErrors.error: Assuming a scaffold is safe because it was used the week before.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the tag and walk the structure each day.

commonErrors.error: Removing a guardrail or brace to get past an obstacle.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not alter the scaffold. Report the obstacle and wait for a competent individual.

commonErrors.error: Standing on a mobile tower while it is being moved.
commonErrors.prevention: Come down before moving it, and lock the wheels before climbing.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a tower is level because it looks level.
commonErrors.prevention: Check verticality and the surface with a level before use.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Warning: do not alter a scaffold. Removing ties, braces, rails or boards can cause collapse. Erection, alteration and dismantling are specialist tasks.

Licence notice: in New South Wales, only licensed scaffolders may erect, alter or dismantle a scaffold where the fall risk exceeds four metres (confirmed in the project licence matrix). This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate or competence to erect, alter or dismantle scaffolding.

Do not use figures from non-Australian sources, such as the green tag and check interval, the stabiliser and tie-off heights, the board minimum and the handrail heights. Use the Australian scaffold standards once checked.
AS 4576 (Guidelines for scaffolding) and the AS/NZS 1576 series are listed as Australian references.
WorkSafe Victoria's scaffolding industry standard page describes practical advice and is not stated as mandatory (checked 2026-11-02). Its legal weight is not stated on the page.

qualityStandard: The tag and certificate are checked before use.
A walk-round is recorded, with any defect found.
A mobile tower is fully checked before anyone climbs.
documentationEvidence: Scaffold or tower check record with tag details
Defect report and stop-work note where use was refused
summary: Only authorised and competent people erect, alter or dismantle scaffolds.
A tag tells you whether a scaffold can be used today, not last week.
Lock the castors and check the base before anyone climbs a mobile tower.
Never remove a rail, brace or board to get past an obstacle.

knowledgeChecks.question: A scaffold tag is out of date. What should happen?
options: The scaffold is used anyway, because the workers have used it before.
It is not used until a competent individual has checked it and the tag is current.
It is used for light work only and the crew is told it is safe to work on
The tag is removed and the work continues and the crew is told it is safe

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of these is a sign that a scaffold must not be used?
options: A handrail is missing on an open edge.
The base is level and fully boarded
The access ladder extends above the landing.
The bracing is in place at every bay.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must a mobile tower's castors be locked before someone climbs it?
options: To make the tower look finished.
So the tower cannot roll or tip while a person is on it.
Because locked castors are required by the colour of the tag.
Locking is needed only for towers above the height the maker sets.

knowledgeChecks.question: What should a scaffold tag show, according to the lesson?
options: Whether it can be used safely, who checked it and when

officialReferences.title: Scaffolds and scaffolding
officialReferences.covers: States that scaffolding work involving a platform with a fall over 4 metres requires a high risk work licence, and that there are three scaffolding licence classes: basic, intermediate and advanced. Gives no tag interval, stabiliser heights or board minimum, and refers readers to a separate guide on inspection and maintenance. Shows no dates. Publisher: Safe Work Australia.

officialReferences.title: Working at heights (SafeWork NSW)
